choices.a: Irreversibly inhibiting the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase of parietal cells
choices.c: Blocking gastrin release from G cells

questions.explanation: Proton pump inhibitors are activated in the acid of the parietal cell's canaliculus and bind the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase covalently, blocking the final step of acid secretion whatever the stimulus. H2 blockers act on one of the three stimuli; antacids neutralize acid.
questions.learning_objective: State the mechanism of proton pump inhibitors.

questions.prompt: A woman had her terminal ileum removed for Crohn disease. Which vitamin deficiency is she at risk of in the coming years?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Stores last years, so deficiency (megaloblastic anemia, neuropathy) appears late; lifelong B12 injections prevent it.
questions.learning_objective: Relate vitamin B12 absorption to intrinsic factor and the terminal ileum.

questions.prompt: A patient with gallstones gets right-upper-quadrant pain after fatty meals. Which hormone links the meal to the pain?

choices.a: Gastrin, released by protein, contracts the gallbladder.
choices.b: Insulin, released by glucose, contracts the gallbladder.
choices.c: Cholecystokinin (CCK), released by fat in the duodenum, contracts the gallbladder.
choices.d: Secretin, released by acid, contracts the gallbladder.

questions.explanation: Fat and protein in the duodenum release CCK from I cells; CCK contracts the gallbladder (and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi). If a stone blocks the cystic duct, the contraction causes biliary colic.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the role of CCK in gallbladder contraction.

questions.prompt: Why does lactase deficiency cause diarrhea after drinking milk?

choices.b: Undigested lactose stays in the gut lumen, drawing water in osmotically, and bacteria ferment it.
choices.c: Lactose triggers an allergic reaction to milk protein.

questions.explanation: Without brush-border lactase, lactose can't be absorbed; it holds water in the lumen (osmotic diarrhea) and colonic bacteria ferment it into gas and short-chain fatty acids, causing bloating. It isn't an allergy.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the mechanism of symptoms in lactase deficiency.

questions.prompt: A man has jaundice, itching, dark urine and pale stools. His conjugated bilirubin is high. Where is the problem?

choices.b: Obstruction of bile flow, such as a stone or tumor in the bile duct
choices.d: Increased bilirubin production in the spleen

questions.explanation: Blocked bile flow backs conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin into the blood; it spills into the urine and darkens it, while little reaches the gut, so stools are pale. Hemolysis and Gilbert syndrome raise unconjugated bilirubin, which is not excreted in urine.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize obstructive (posthepatic) jaundice from its features.

questions.prompt: A healthy 20-year-old notices yellow eyes after a few days of the flu and not eating. Unconjugated bilirubin is mildly raised; blood count and liver enzymes are normal. The most likely explanation is:

choices.c: Obstruction of the common bile duct

questions.explanation: Gilbert syndrome is a common, benign reduction in UGT1A1 activity; fasting, illness and stress raise unconjugated bilirubin mildly. Normal hemoglobin argues against hemolysis and normal enzymes against hepatitis.

questions.prompt: A 19-year-old took a large overdose of acetaminophen four hours ago and feels well. Her level is above the treatment line. What is the antidote, and how does it work?

choices.c: N-acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione to neutralize NAPQI

questions.explanation: N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione (and supports sulfation), detoxifying NAPQI. It is most effective within 8–10 hours of ingestion, before liver injury appears, which is why a patient who looks well still needs it.
questions.learning_objective: Explain N-acetylcysteine treatment of acetaminophen overdose.
